title: Non-invasive ventilation and high flow nasal oxygen

steps.tx: In **FLORALI**, **high flow nasal oxygen** did not clearly cut intubation in the whole group, but 90 day mortality was lower than with **non-invasive ventilation** or standard oxygen in acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure. High flow delivers heated humidified gas up to 60 L/min, washing out nasopharyngeal dead space and generating modest positive end-expiratory pressure.

steps.tx: The **ROX index** is SpO2 over FiO2, divided by respiratory rate. A value below 3.85 at 12 hours predicts high flow failure. A value above 4.88 suggests success. Serial calculation of this ratio at 2, 6, and 12 hours identifies failing patients early, preventing delayed emergent intubation associated with increased ICU mortality.

steps.tx: **Non-invasive ventilation** is first line for a **COPD exacerbation** with **respiratory acidosis** when the pH is about 7.25 to 7.35, and for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema treated with **CPAP**. Bilevel pressure support unloads fatigued ventilatory muscles, lowers arterial carbon dioxide tension, and markedly reduces the need for invasive mechanical ventilation in acute hypercapnic respiratory failure.

left.title: COPD exacerbation NIV
points: Indicated for acute respiratory acidosis with pH 7.25 to 7.35
Provides inspiratory pressure support to augment tidal volume
Reduces work of breathing and lowers mortality

right.title: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema CPAP
points: Continuous positive pressure recruits fluid-filled alveoli
Reduces left ventricular afterload and increases compliance
Rapidly relieves acute dyspnoea without invasive tube

steps.tx: **Helmet non-invasive ventilation** can deliver prolonged pressure support with less skin breakdown than a face mask. It still needs a clear plan for intubation if work of breathing stays high. The transparent helmet interface seals around the neck, enabling higher positive end-expiratory pressures with minimal air leaks while avoiding nasal bridge pressure ulceration.

rows: Zero nasal bridge pressure; permits high PEEP
Requires high fresh gas flow to avoid CO2 rebreathing
Prone to facial skin necrosis and substantial air leakage
Urgent escalation if tachypnoea and accessory muscle use persist

steps.tx: **Patient self inflicted lung injury** is vigorous spontaneous breathing that overdistends and swings pleural pressure. It is a reason to intubate or deepen sedation, not to watch a tiring patient on high flow. Enormous transpulmonary pressure swings generate cyclic pendelluft gas movement, vascular engorgement, and worsening pulmonary vascular permeability oedema.

left.title: P-SILI pathophysiology
points: Excessive neuroventilatory drive produces high tidal volumes
Large negative pleural swings amplify lung strain
Pendelluft shifts gas between dependent and non-dependent zones

right.title: Clinical management strategy
points: Prompt intubation and controlled mechanical ventilation
Neuromuscular blockade or deeper sedation abolishes swings
Prevents irreversible progression to severe biotrauma

steps.tx: After extubation, high flow or non-invasive ventilation prevents **reintubation** in high risk patients, including those with hypercapnia or heart failure. Routine non-invasive ventilation in low risk patients can delay a needed reintubation. Prophylactic application in patients over 65 years provides proven benefit and decreases extubation failure within 48 hours.

rows: High risk: hypercapnia, age over 65, heart failure

steps.tx: The **HACOR score** is used to combine heart rate, acidosis, consciousness, oxygenation, and respiratory rate to flag non-invasive ventilation failure. A rising score is a prompt to intubate. Assessing the HACOR score within the first two hours of non-invasive support accurately stratifies patients who are unlikely to succeed, preventing catastrophic sudden respiratory arrest.

left.title: HACOR components
points: Oxygenation ratio PaO2/FiO2 and respiratory rate

right.title: Clinical utility
points: Score above 5 at 1 to 2 hours predicts failure

steps.tx: **Awake prone positioning** improves oxygenation in hypoxaemic patients who are not intubated. It is not a substitute for intubation when work of breathing is unsustainable. Prone posture promotes dorsal lung alveolar recruitment, improves ventilation-perfusion matching, and decreases ventilation heterogeneity, but persistent severe retractions require prompt invasive airway protection.
